opus-5.5.text:
I think there's enormous potential there, and it's honestly one of the areas I'm most excited about right now. A lot of the conversation in AI for biology focuses on building bigger models or training on more data, and that's important. But I think we're underappreciating how much knowledge is already latent inside the models we have.

Take protein language models, or models trained on single-cell gene expression data. These models are trained to do something fairly simple: predict a masked amino acid, or reconstruct gene expression profiles. But to do that well across millions of examples, they have to internalize a lot of real biology. They pick up things like structural constraints, which residues co-evolve, which genes tend to be co-regulated, which pathways respond together under perturbation. Nobody explicitly taught them those things. They emerged as a byproduct of the training objective.

So the question becomes: can we go in and actually read that knowledge out, in a form that's useful to scientists? Not just using the model as a black-box predictor, but treating it almost like a new kind of experimental system that we can probe and interrogate.

There are a few ways to do this. One is interpretability work. Using methods like sparse autoencoders, you can decompose a model's internal representations into features, and some of those features turn out to correspond to meaningful biological concepts, like binding sites, secondary structure motifs, or particular cell states. Sometimes you find features that don't map cleanly onto anything we have a name for, and those are the interesting ones, because they might point to biology we haven't characterized yet.

Another approach is in silico perturbation. You take a model of cells, computationally knock out a gene or tweak an input, and see how the model's predictions shift. That generates hypotheses about gene function or drug response much faster and more cheaply than running wet lab experiments for every possibility. You still need to validate in the lab, but it helps you prioritize which experiments are worth running.

And then there's the angle of using large language models, which have read huge amounts of the scientific literature, as a kind of knowledge base. They can connect findings across papers and fields in ways an individual researcher might not, simply because no one person can read everything.

I do want to add a note of caution, though. Just because a model has learned something doesn't mean it learned the right thing. Models can pick up spurious correlations, batch effects, or biases in how data was collected. So extracting knowledge has to go together with rigorous validation. The goal isn't to trust the model blindly. It's to use it as a hypothesis generator that makes the scientific process more efficient.

But overall, I think we're sitting on a goldmine. We've spent a lot of compute and data training these models, and we've only scratched the surface of understanding what they actually know.

r001.rationale: The candidate says existing models contain latent biological knowledge and that probing their features could reveal biology not yet characterized.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is one of the most exciting and underappreciated directions in the field right now. We've spent the last few years training these enormous models on huge amounts of scientific text, protein sequences, gene expression data, and so on, and the natural question is: what have they actually learned? These models aren't just pattern-matching on surface tokens. In many cases they've internalized real structure about biology, relationships between genes, pathways, cell types, disease mechanisms, that no single human has fully synthesized because the literature is simply too vast.

So one potential is to treat the model as a kind of knowledge repository that we can query systematically. Instead of reading ten thousand papers about a particular gene, we can ask the model to summarize what's known, propose hypotheses about function, or predict how a perturbation might propagate through a cell. We've done work along these lines, for example using language models to generate gene embeddings or to annotate cell types and pathways, and what's striking is how often the model recovers biology that was never explicitly spelled out in any one source. It's connecting dots across the corpus.

The second potential, which I find even more interesting, is using these models as hypothesis generators for experiments. Biology is bottlenecked on which experiments to run. If a model can propose plausible targets or combinations of perturbations and we can then test them in the lab, you get a closed loop where the model's extracted knowledge directly accelerates discovery. We've seen early versions of this in virtual cell work, where the model predicts transcriptional responses to perturbations it's never seen, and then those predictions guide what you actually screen.

Now I want to be careful. These models also hallucinate, and biology is a domain where confident wrong answers are costly. So a big part of extracting knowledge responsibly is building ways to calibrate the model's confidence, trace its claims back to evidence, and benchmark it against held-out experimental ground truth rather than against text. When you do that carefully, you find there's a lot of genuine signal to mine. I think the next few years will be about turning these models from passive encyclopedias into active collaborators that help us decide what to measure next.

r001.rationale: The response says existing models have internalized biological structure and can connect information across sources to recover biology not explicitly stated in any one source, revealing insights to mine.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential here, because these models have learned patterns from much more data than any individual scientist could look at. The interesting question is whether we can turn those patterns into insights that we can understand and test.

For example, if a model is very good at predicting a protein’s function, we can ask what features of the protein are driving that prediction. Does it identify a particular sequence or an interaction that we hadn’t appreciated before? That could give us a hypothesis to take into the lab.

But we have to distinguish between extracting something the model has memorized from the literature and discovering a relationship that actually generalizes. So I see this as a loop: interrogate the model, generate a hypothesis, test it experimentally, and use those results to refine our understanding. The model’s prediction is a starting point for science, rather than the conclusion.

r001.rationale: The response says existing models have learned patterns from extensive data that can be turned into testable insights, including previously unappreciated biological hypotheses.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential here, because these models may have learned useful biological patterns that we don’t yet know how to articulate. Usually, we ask a model to make a prediction: What does this protein do? How might this mutation affect its function? But we can also ask what the model has learned that could help us generate a new scientific hypothesis.

For example, if a model consistently predicts that certain mutations have similar effects, we could investigate whether those mutations share an underlying mechanism. That could point us toward a relationship that wasn’t obvious from looking at individual experiments.

The important step is turning that pattern into something specific and testable. A model’s prediction isn’t itself a biological discovery. But if we can extract a hypothesis, design an experiment, and validate it, then the model becomes a tool for discovery, helping us decide which experiments are most informative to do next.

r001.rationale: The response says existing models may have learned useful biological patterns and that extracting them into testable hypotheses could reveal relationships or insights not obvious from existing experiments.
